title: impCubeVolume::frame is never initialised, so a poisoned stack slot yields a surface of garbage indices
description:
impCubeVolume::frame is an unsigned short declared at impCubeVolume.h:92. The constructor assigns surface, surfacevalue, fastnormals and crawlfromsides and calls init(); it never assigns frame. The only other write anywhere is 'frame++' at the top of each makeSurface overload.

init() zeroes every per-cube generation counter -- cube_frame, corner_frame, x/y/z_vertex_frame -- at impCubeVolume.cpp:89-93. So the cache-hit test in addVertexToSurface, 'cubes[index].x_vertex_frame == frame', compares a zeroed field against an uninitialised one.

If frame happens to start at 0xFFFF, frame++ wraps to 0 and every edge in the volume reports a cache hit on the very first makeSurface(). addVertexToSurface then takes the early-return branch, calls surface->addIndex(cubes[index].x_vertex_index) -- which init() does NOT zero, so it is also garbage -- and never calls addVertex at all.

REPRODUCED, not inferred. Placement-new over a buffer memset to 0xFF:

  with frame poisoned to 0xFFFF: vertices=0 indices=1752

1752 indices into a zero-length vertex array. Every one of them out of range.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE NOW. This is pre-existing and has been harmless in the savers, which allocate one volume on the heap at startup and would have to be very unlucky. ss-or3 changed the exposure: tests/test_impcubevolume.cpp constructs eleven volumes, most of them on the stack, where the slot's previous contents are whatever the last call left there. That is a 1-in-65536 flake per construction that turns the coverage gate red for reasons no one will be able to reproduce.

And it compounds with ss-c4f: the area and manifold cases dereference getVertex(getIndex(t)) without bounds-checking, so this state does not produce a clean assertion failure -- it reads unmapped memory and takes the whole test binary down, which coverage.sh reports as a build/config error rather than a test failure.

THE FIX is one line, 'frame = 0;' in the constructor. Worth also zeroing x_vertex_index/y_vertex_index/z_vertex_index in init(), which are read on the cache-hit path and never initialised, so that a future generation-counter bug degrades to wrong-but-in-range rather than out-of-range.

Found by the independent review pass on helios#10 / hyperspace#8, after those merged. Identical in both twins.

## Steps to Reproduce

Placement-new an impCubeVolume into a buffer filled with 0xFF, configure any field, call init() and makeSurface(). getVertexCount() returns 0 while getIndexCount() returns the full index count.

## Acceptance Criteria

frame is initialised in the constructor, the poisoned-storage reproduction returns a normal surface, and both twins carry the fix.
notes:
CORRECTION to the description above: it cites 'ss-c4f' for the bounds-check gap it compounds with. That ID does not exist -- it was written before the companion work was filed. The gap is real and is in tests/test_impcubevolume.cpp, where the closed-manifold and triangulated-area cases call getVertex(getIndex(t)) without checking the index against getVertexCount(). The index-validity assertion lives in a different case, and harness_fail records and continues rather than aborting, so a bad index is dereferenced rather than reported. It is being fixed in the follow-up to helios#10 / hyperspace#8, not under a separate issue.

The compounding is the point worth keeping: this bug produces exactly the state -- a full index array over zero vertices -- that turns that unchecked dereference into a read of unmapped memory. On its own each is survivable; together they take the gate down with an error coverage.sh reports as a build failure rather than a test failure.

title: The branch guard checks the wrong repo for 'cd <submodule> && git commit'
description:
The guard CLAUDE.md calls enforcement is bypassed by the most natural way an agent enters a submodule.

.claude/hooks/guard-default-branch.py resolves the repository as os.path.join(cwd, repo_arg) where cwd is the Bash payload's cwd -- the SESSION directory. A 'cd' earlier in the same command line does not move it. So 'cd helios && git commit' is checked against the superproject's branch, never helios'.

Proven by probe, with hills on master (its default branch):

  git -C hills commit -m test   -> refuse | commit on master in hills
  cd hills && git commit -m test -> allow  | commit in screen-savers on test/coverage-helios

The allow is not a near miss: the guard never looked at hills at all. It read the superproject's branch, found test/coverage-helios, and passed it.

This is not hypothetical. During the first /coverage-loop run (ss-1gl), 6 of the 8 test commits made inside helios logged 'commit in screen-savers on test/coverage-helios'. Every one of them landed in helios on test/coverage-loop. The guard was checking the wrong repository for the entire wave, and would not have stopped a commit on helios' master.

It matters most exactly where the policy is hardest to follow: the submodule half of the two-PR workflow, where CLAUDE.md warns 'never commit inside a submodule while it is in detached HEAD'.

Related but distinct from ss-mqv, which is about a switch in the same compound command; this is about cd. Both are the same root cause -- the parser reads the command as text and the resolver reads state from before it runs.

Fix directions: track cd within the command when resolving the repo, or resolve per-git-call by asking git itself (git rev-parse --show-toplevel from the effective directory), or refuse a commit whose effective repo cannot be determined rather than falling back to cwd.
acceptance_criteria: 'cd <submodule> && git commit' on the submodule's default branch is refused; a probe covering cd, git -C, and the plain form is recorded so the fix cannot regress silently
close_reason:
Fixed: the guard now tracks cd across the command line, so a git call is resolved against the directory it will actually run in rather than the payload's session cwd.

cd hills && git commit, with hills on master, now refuses and names hills. Before the fix it allowed, reporting 'commit in screen-savers on <branch>' -- the superproject's branch, for a commit landing in the submodule.

A cd is applied whatever separator precedes it, and only if the target exists: a cd that would fail leaves the shell where it was under ';' and short-circuits the rest under '&&', so either way not applying it is right.

Pinned by .claude/hooks/test_guard_default_branch.py -- 16 cases, standard library only, temp repos so results do not depend on what branch the checkout is on. 7 fail against the pre-fix hook, all cd-dependent; the other 9 are the forms that already worked, there so the fix cannot regress them. Run with: python3 .claude/hooks/test_guard_default_branch.py

Deliberately NOT fixed alongside: ss-mqv. Tracking a switch is not symmetric with tracking a cd. Whether a directory exists is a question about the filesystem and can be asked; whether 'git switch -c' will succeed is not, so assuming it would is how a commit reaches a default branch across a ';'. ss-mqv still fails safe and still costs a retry.

ss-jl7 -- the two commits with no guard record at all -- is untouched and remains the reason a short hook count cannot be diagnosed.

Canon updated: docs/reference/tooling.md's guard section now describes cd tracking and its Known limit block covers only ss-jl7 and ss-mqv. I12 moved to Landed, L4-F2 status-marked closed.

title: Run /coverage-loop once, end to end, on one submodule
description: The loop has never executed: no loop-log.json, no queue.json. Every stage is an untested assumption, including the marginal-gain stop rule which reads a file that has never existed. helios has 675 uncovered bucket-A regions, so there is no shortage of input. Goal is not coverage; it is finding out whether the machinery works. From L3-F1/L3-F2.
close_reason:
Ran end to end on helios, 2026-08-21. 20.89% -> 63.54% lines (496 -> 1506 of 2370), addressable ceiling 26.95% -> 51.8%, 49 -> 158 cases. Eight test commits in helios PR #7, pointer bump and ratchet in superproject PR #25, both merged.

The goal was not coverage, it was finding out whether the machinery works. It does, and it produced ten issues:

- ss-1sp (P1) the branch guard checks the wrong repo for 'cd <sub> && git commit', so it covered none of the wave's eight submodule commits
- ss-jl7 two of those eight produced no guard record at all, not reproducible
- ss-e5n nine undiscriminating paths inside otherwise-real tests, found by the verifier and extended by two independent review passes
- ss-9wk, ss-c6g two production defects found while characterizing
- ss-53x, ss-hye the read-only coverage-runner wrote into the submodule tree, via a --json footgun that bit four separate agents in one run
- ss-05i, ss-07o rule_would_say attribution, found reviewing the fix that preceded the run

Three things the run established about the loop itself, all recorded in .claude/artifacts/loop-log.json:

1. The threshold argument is unreachable on helios by construction. addressable keeps ss-aio's 525 GL-blocked regions in the denominator while they cannot be covered, capping the submodule near 48%.
2. Stage 5's addressable formula divides a line count by a region denominator. The real figure came from re-running the classifier.
3. The marginal-gain floor STILL has never executed -- the queue emptied in one iteration, so the stop rule this issue most wanted to exercise remains untested. A second run, on hyperspace, would be the way to reach it.

title: xcodebuild cannot open a project on this machine, blocking all phase 2 work
description:
xcodebuild fails to load a required plug-in and exits 70 on any project operation. Found by trying to start ss-2d6.

  xcodebuild -version                              works -- Xcode 26.6, build 17F113
  xcodebuild -project helios/Helios.xcodeproj -list  exit 70
  xcrun clang --version                            works -- Apple clang 21.0.0

The error is a dlopen failure on IDESimulatorFoundation: a missing Swift symbol in DVTDownloads, with xcodebuild's own advice being to run 'xcodebuild -runFirstLaunch'.

Scope of the damage, which is narrower than it first looks but blocks exactly the wrong thing:

NOT affected -- the coverage gate and everything phase 1 built. tools/coverage.sh drives xcrun clang directly and never touches xcodebuild, which is why every test, every kill-check and every gate run this session worked.

BLOCKED -- everything in phase 2. Raising the deployment target (ss-2d6), all three Metal ports, and the host-layer work all mean editing Xcode projects, and none of it can be verified locally while xcodebuild cannot open one. Changing MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET across three projects with no way to build them afterwards is not a change worth making.

FIX, and it needs the machine's owner: run 'xcodebuild -runFirstLaunch'. It usually needs sudo, which is why it is not done here.
design: Worth noting what this says about the harness rather than just the machine. Phase 1 was buildable entirely through xcrun clang, so it never depended on a working xcodebuild and never noticed it was broken. Phase 2 depends on it completely from its first commit. The submodule CI workflows have the same shape -- they compile with clang and would stay green through this, so CI will not catch it either.
acceptance_criteria: xcodebuild -project <any>.xcodeproj -list exits 0.
close_reason: Fixed by running 'xcodebuild -runFirstLaunch', which completed without sudo -- the assumption that it would need elevation was wrong and untested. All three projects now open: xcodebuild -list exits 0 for Helios, Hills and Hyperspace. Phase 2 is unblocked.

title: Modernize the macOS platform layer in all three savers
description:
The Metal ports replace the rendering path. This is everything else the phrase 'macOS related updates' covers, and it applies identically to all three.

Measured 2026-08-21, same in helios, hills and hyperspace:

  MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET  10.9  -- from 2013, and it constrains every API choice below it
  NSOpenGLView                    -- deprecated since 10.14; 2 files per repo reference it
  ScreenSaverView                 -- 1 file per repo; the modern host API has moved on

Work this implies, to be confirmed per repo rather than assumed:

  raise the deployment target to something current, and decide what that costs in supported OS versions
  replace NSOpenGLView hosting with a Metal-backed view
  bring the ScreenSaverView subclass up to the current API, including the preferences sheet
  Xcode project settings: SDK, architectures (Apple silicon), build settings that predate them
  signing and notarization, which a .saver bundle now needs to install cleanly

Deliberately not folded into the three port issues. Those are about rendering and geometry, where the characterization tests apply; this is host integration, where they do not, and mixing the two makes a failed test ambiguous.
design: Sequence relative to the ports is a real decision and is not made here. Raising the deployment target first would simplify each port by making modern Metal APIs available; doing it after keeps the ports as pure renderer changes. Worth deciding once, for all three, before the first port branch opens.
notes:
FIRST HALF DONE 2026-08-21, merged in all three subrepos and pinned in screen-savers PR #20.

Target is macOS 26.0 against the 26.5 SDK, per the instruction to take the latest. Not the 10.11 that would minimally compile -- 26 means every API the Metal port wants is unconditionally available, with no availability guards or fallback paths to write and then delete.

The finding that changed this issue's character: the savers did not build at all. Every target failed on 'SDK does not contain libarclite', removed in Xcode 14.3 and needed only for ARC below 10.11, so the 10.9 target was incompatible with any current toolchain. hills failed again underneath that on 'ld: framework AGL not found' -- the Carbon-era framework, linked by both targets and referenced nowhere in the source. So this was repair, not modernization, and it was blocking phase 2 outright.

All four targets now build Release: Helios, Hyperspace, Hills Screensaver, Hills Application.

SECOND HALF STILL OPEN, and it is the part entangled with each port:
  NSOpenGLView replacement with a Metal-backed view
  the ScreenSaverView subclass and its preferences sheet
  signing and notarization -- currently failing for want of a Developer ID certificate for team 8D98N325TG on this machine, and deliberately untouched since changing signing settings blind could break the release path

Consider closing this issue once #20 merges and re-filing the second half per-saver, since ss-q1r stage 5 already accounts for hills' share of it and the same will be true for the other two.

title: Define and hold the phase 1 to phase 2 gate
description:
"When enough code coverage has been accomplished, begin modernizing" needs a definition, or it becomes either a stall or a rubber stamp. This issue is that definition.

The wrong gate is a percentage. helios and hyperspace measure a 986-region denominator that is the shared C++ core only; hills measures 31 regions because Camera.m is the only non-GL, non-Cocoa unit it has. Driving those to 100% would leave Helios.cpp, rsText and HeliosView.mm -- the actual screen saver -- untested, because they are not in the denominator. A percentage of a denominator the port itself will redefine is not a gate.

The right gate is a safety net. Phase 2 changes the rendering path. What must not change is the geometry and colour that path consumes. So:

GATE, per submodule:

1. The modules the port feeds are characterized well enough that a change in their output fails a test. For helios and hyperspace that is impCubeVolume (makeSurface, polygonize, crawl_sort, crawl_nosort, calculateCornerMask, addVertexToSurface), impCubeTables, Rgbhsl and rsMath. impCubeTables, Rgbhsl and rsMath are done; impCubeVolume is not, and it is the bulk of what remains -- see ss-or3.

2. Bucket B is cleared or consciously waived, in writing. helios currently has 10 functions and 47 regions that need a refactor before they can be tested. Some of those refactors ARE the port, so waiving them into phase 2 is a legitimate answer -- silently leaving them is not.

3. Every new test survives a kill-check. Coverage that cannot fail is not a safety net, and this project has already caught itself writing three such tests.

Numeric proxy, useful but secondary: addressable ceiling of 80% for helios and hyperspace. Currently 25.9% each. It is a proxy because criterion 1 is what actually matters.

hills passes this gate today, trivially and for the wrong-looking reason: its only testable unit is covered and everything else is blocked on its port. hills is therefore free to start phase 2 now, and it is the submodule where porting buys the most coverage.
design:
Criterion 1 is named-modules rather than a number because the denominator is not stable across the phase boundary -- porting moves files into scope, so the percentage can fall while the codebase gets better. Anything gated on the percentage alone would misread that as a regression.

The gate is per-submodule on purpose. hills is ready and helios and hyperspace are not, and forcing them to move together would either hold hills back or start the C++ ports early.
acceptance_criteria: A written per-submodule verdict on all three criteria, recorded in this issue, before any port branch is opened for that submodule.
notes:
CRITERION 1 WAIVED 2026-08-21, by the decision on ss-aio.

The gate as written required the modules the port feeds to be characterized, naming impCubeVolume. That cannot be done: impSurface calls glGenBuffers from its constructor, so neither class is constructible without a GL context, and the fix was folded into the ports rather than made now.

A criterion that cannot be met is not a gate, it is a stall. So criterion 1 is waived for helios and hyperspace, and the obligation moves into the port issues: decouple impSurface from GL early, then characterize impCubeVolume before rewriting the geometry path.

RESULTING VERDICT -- the gate passes for all three submodules.

helios and hyperspace: criterion 1 waived as above. Criterion 2 satisfied (ss-73x: every bucket B group has a written verdict). Criterion 3 holding (every case this session kill-checked, and the discipline caught three weak tests and two bad mutations).
hills: passed already and for the same underlying reason -- its coverage is blocked on its port.

Phase 2 is open. What phase 1 delivered is the harness, the gate mechanics, and characterization of everything that could be reached without a GL context: rsMath, the marching-cubes lookup tables, Rgbhsl, Camera, and the free vector helpers. What it could not deliver is the geometry pipeline, and that is now the ports' first obligation rather than an omission.
close_reason:
Verdict rendered for all three submodules: the gate passes, and phase 2 is open.

helios and hyperspace -- criterion 1 waived by the ss-aio decision, since impCubeVolume is unconstructible without a GL context and the fix was folded into the ports. Criterion 2 satisfied via ss-73x. Criterion 3 holding.
hills -- passed already; its remaining coverage is blocked on its port.

The issue's purpose was to make 'enough coverage' a definition rather than a stall or a rubber stamp, and it did that: it forced the impCubeVolume blocker into the open before a port started on top of it, and it turned criterion 1 from an unmeetable requirement into a recorded obligation on the port issues rather than a silent omission.

What the gate could not deliver is worth stating in its own closure: the geometry pipeline is NOT characterized, and the ports proceed without that safety net by explicit decision.

title: Phase 1 - a harness and coverage good enough to port against
description:
Goal one of two: build an effective test harness and raise coverage.

Done as of 2026-08-21: tools/coverage.sh (ratchet gate), tools/triage.sh (A/B/C classifier), /coverage-loop and its agents and skills, a PreToolUse branch guard, per-submodule CI, branch protection on the three forks, and a single-binary test harness with drivers in all three repos. Coverage went 0% -> 19.6% in helios and hyperspace and 0% -> 94.3% in hills.

What phase 1 still owes is NOT a bigger percentage. It is a safety net: enough characterized behaviour that phase 2 can change the rendering path and find out immediately if it changed anything else. See the gate issue for what that means concretely.

Read the numbers with their denominators. helios and hyperspace measure 986 regions -- the shared C++ core that compiles without a GL context. hills measures 31, because Camera.m is the only unit that is not GL or Cocoa coupled. Those denominators are not the screen savers; they are the part of the screen savers that is testable before the port.
design: This epic cannot reach the whole codebase on its own, and that is the finding that reshapes both goals. Coverage is capped by un-ported code: every coverage/<name>.json _scope block excludes the GL-coupled files and says the scope should grow as the port replaces them. Driving the current denominators to 100% would still leave Helios.cpp, rsText and HeliosView.mm untested, because they are not in the denominator.

title: Cut the two redundant coverage builds out of /coverage-loop
description:
Every iteration of /coverage-loop runs the instrumented build two more times than it needs to, and tools/coverage.sh wipes and rebuilds .coverage-build/<submodule>/ on every invocation, so each one is a full rebuild.

First: Stage 5 measures twice. verifier.md step 1 runs ./tools/coverage.sh --no-notify <submodule>, then coverage-loop.md line 139 re-dispatches coverage-runner, which runs the identical command against a tree nothing touched in between.

Second: Stage 1 re-measures an untouched tree. On iterations after the first, nothing changes between Stage 5 measuring and the next Stage 1 measuring again.

Fix both: have the verifier emit coverage-runner's report block (STATUS / pct / baseline / BASELINE_MOVED) from the run it already did and delete the Stage 5 re-dispatch; and have Stage 1 measure only on iteration 1, with later iterations reading the previous entry's coverage value out of loop-log.json.
design: Folding the measurement into the verifier does not violate the never-grade-your-own-work rule: the verifier is read-only and authored nothing in the wave. A reviewer who reproduced the gate green from a clean state is stronger evidence than a separate agent's number, not weaker. This is the largest wall-clock win available in the harness and is most of why a 3-iteration cap feels expensive.
acceptance_criteria: One gate run per iteration boundary instead of three. Stage 5 dispatches the verifier only. Stage 1 reads loop-log on iterations 2 and 3.
close_reason: Closed

title: Build the /coverage-loop pipeline: command, agents, skills, hooks
description: Replace ad-hoc skill invocation with an explicit orchestrated loop. A /coverage-loop slash command drives five scoped subagents (coverage-runner, triager, test-writer, refactorer, verifier) that follow four skills (coverage, triage, testing, refactor). Skills hold domain procedure, agents hold execution context and tool allowlists, the command holds the loop. Hooks in .claude/settings.json enforce the branch policy and syntax-check test edits.
design: Adapted to this repo rather than the generic design: tools/coverage.sh and tools/triage.sh are the runner and classifier, coverage/<name>.triage.json is the existing A/B/C contract so the triager selects from it rather than re-deriving it, the loop threshold is measured against the addressable ceiling not raw coverage, and test work happens on a branch inside the submodule (two PRs per the branch policy).
acceptance_criteria: /coverage-loop exists and runs; five agent definitions with scoped tools; testing and refactor skills written; hooks wired and executable; all four repos' branch policy respected by the loop.
close_reason:
Merged as fiazsami/screen-savers PR #7. The pipeline is built and has since been corrected against two independent audits: the command file, five agents, four skills and two hooks, with the redundant per-iteration rebuilds removed, the stop rule moved onto loop-log data, the verifier's restraint made checkable and routed through a different model, and the exit path fixed to re-attach submodules, stage the ledgers and carry evidence in the PR body.

It has also now been exercised end to end by hand rather than only reasoned about: the harness, drivers, gate, baselines, ledgers and two-PR submodule flow all ran for real this session across all three submodules.

title: Apply the branch policy to the three subrepos
description: With the policy established in the root repo, apply it to helios, hills, and hyperspace: enable GitHub branch protection on each master (require a PR, no direct pushes), and add a short AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md pointer in each so an agent working inside a submodule sees the rule without reading the superproject. Requires gh auth.
close_reason:
Both halves done. Branch protection is enabled on master in helios, hills and hyperspace: PR required (0 approvals), the 'tests' status check required, force pushes and deletions refused, enforce_admins off so a solo owner cannot lock themselves out. Verified by reading the protection back from all three. The AGENTS.md pointer landed in each repo via fiazsami/helios#3, hills#2 and hyperspace#2 -- it states the rules invisible from inside a submodule: never commit to master, pass -R to gh because these are forks and gh otherwise resolves to the parent, never commit from a detached HEAD, and a change here is two PRs with the pointer taking the merge commit rather than the branch tip.

Requiring a check meant first building one: there was no CI anywhere, so requiring a check would have made every PR unmergeable. .github/workflows/tests.yml now builds and runs each suite, green on real CI in all three repos before protection was turned on.

title: impCubeVolume's crawl-and-sort paths are still uncovered after ss-or3
description:
ss-or3 took impCubeVolume.cpp from 7.1% to 58.8% and characterized the pipeline against analytic geometry. It did not finish the job, and the remainder is concentrated and cheap.

MEASURED from coverage/helios.triage.json after ss-or3 merged (helios#10, hyperspace#8). Bucket A still holds 242 uncovered regions across 6 functions, and three of them are 239 of that:

  119  impCubeVolume::makeSurface(float, float, float, impCrawlPointVector&)
   92  impCubeVolume::makeSurface(impCrawlPointVector&)
   28  impCubeVolume::crawl_sort(unsigned, unsigned, unsigned)

The cause for two of them is simply that the tests never call them:

  tests/test_impcubevolume.cpp calls makeSurface(), makeSurface(eye) and
  makeSurface(cpv). It never calls the four-argument makeSurface(eye, cpv).
  That overload is 119/119 uncovered -- not one region -- and it is the only
  caller of crawl_sort, which is why crawl_sort is 28/28.

  setCrawlFromSides() is never called either, so every crawlfromsides branch
  in the crawl is unreached. That is most of why makeSurface(cpv) sits at
  24/116 covered despite being called three times: a single seed at the centre
  of one ball walks one path through a function full of conditionals.

WHAT TO DO. Extend the existing file rather than starting a new one -- the sphere field, the derived h^2/4 bound and the two-disjoint-balls fixture all apply unchanged, and the existing cases already show how to assert relations rather than run output.

  1. The four-argument overload, with the same geometric assertions the other
     three overloads get. It should agree with makeSurface(cpv) on geometry and
     with makeSurface(eye) on ordering -- both are relational, neither is a
     golden count.
  2. setCrawlFromSides(true) against the same two-ball field. Crawling from the
     sides is a different traversal that must reach the same surface, which is
     exactly the kind of invariant this file is built around.
  3. More than one seed placement, so the crawl's branching is exercised rather
     than one lucky path.

Every new case must survive the kill-check, and the mutants from ss-or3 are reusable as-is -- particularly "crawl overload falls back to exhaustive", which the four-argument overload currently has no case to catch.

Not folded into ss-or3's PRs because they were already merged when this was measured, and because it is a clean increment rather than a correction.
acceptance_criteria: The four-argument makeSurface overload and the crawlfromsides branches are exercised, bucket A's uncovered region count in impCubeVolume.cpp is materially below 242, and every new case is kill-checked in both twins.

title: Triage ledger has no way to expire a human verdict
description:
tools/triage_classify.py build_entries() carries a human verdict forward on every run, forever:

    if earlier and earlier.get("set_by") == "human":
        entry["verdict"] = earlier["verdict"]

There is no --clear. Once a function has been --set, the rules can never speak for it again, no matter how much the source changes underneath. rule_would_say records the disagreement, which is good, but nothing acts on it and nothing expires it.

Found by hitting it. ss-aio reclassified 20 functions A -> B by hand because impSurface's constructor called glGenBuffers and made them transitively unconstructible. The fix for ss-aio removes that coupling entirely, so all 20 are testable again -- but a re-run of tools/triage.sh moved only ONE function, impSurface::impSurface() itself, because that one had a rule verdict rather than a human one. The other 20 stayed B with rule_would_say: a:pure sitting next to them, saying in the ledger that the rules disagree, and changing nothing.

So the ledger's headline counts were wrong in the direction that hides work: 22 B / 124 A when the truth after the fix is closer to 2 B / 144 A. An agent reading bucket A to find work would have been told there was almost none.

The three options, in the order I'd rank them:

1. A --clear FUNC verb that drops set_by/reason/decided and lets the rules recompute. Smallest, and it matches how --set already works.
2. Expire a human verdict automatically when rule_would_say has persisted across N runs, or when the function's source hash changes. Stronger, and it means nobody has to remember.
3. Leave it and require the human to --set the new verdict explicitly. This is the status quo and it is what I had to do; it works but it records "a human decided A" when the truth is "the rules decide A and the human no longer has an opinion", which is a different and less useful fact.

Related to ss-05i and ss-07o, which are both about rule_would_say being stale or wrong. This is the third instance and the mechanism is shared.

## Steps to Reproduce

Take any entry with set_by=human whose rule_would_say disagrees. Change the source so the rules would now produce the human's original verdict's opposite. Re-run tools/triage.sh. The verdict does not move.

## Acceptance Criteria

A function whose human verdict has been overtaken by a source change can be returned to rule control without hand-editing coverage/<name>.triage.json, and the bucket counts reflect it.

title: A writer satisfied Stage 3's clean-tree rule by reverting Stage 2's output
description:
Observed in the hyperspace run (ss-44s), recorded in .claude/artifacts/loop-log.json: 'TRIAGE LEDGER WAS DESTROYED MID-RUN and had to be regenerated. A writer ran git checkout on coverage/hyperspace.triage.json in the superproject to keep its tree clean, reverting Stage 2's output to main's pre-wave version.'

The writer was not misbehaving. It was doing what it was told. Stage 3 says to keep the tree clean and stop the loop if it is not, and coverage/<name>.triage.json is a superproject file that Stage 2 had just rewritten -- so from inside the dispatch it looks exactly like stray dirt. Reverting it is the obvious way to satisfy the rule.

The conflict is the same shape as ss-p1m: a rule forbids the state that an earlier stage of the same run is required to create. Stage 0's clean-tree check already carries an exemption list for coverage/*.triage.json and coverage/*.baseline.json. Stage 3's does not, and no instruction tells a writer that the ledger is live run state rather than dirt.

Why it matters beyond the inconvenience: the ledger is the evidence for what the run declined to test. The exit path needs it, ss-53w's criterion 2 -- 'bucket B is cleared or consciously waived, in writing' -- is satisfied by it, and the baseline commit carries it as the record of the run's own scope decisions. Regenerating it after the fact reconstructs the verdicts from a post-wave measurement, which is not the same artifact: any verdict set by hand during the run (this run set impCubeTables::nextedge to C) is silently lost.

FIX: carry Stage 0's exemption list into Stage 3, and state positively that coverage/*.triage.json is run state a writer must not touch -- neither edit nor revert. The exemption exists once already; the defect is that it was not propagated to the stage where writers actually run.
acceptance_criteria: Stage 3's cleanliness rule names the same exemptions as Stage 0's, and says explicitly that the triage ledger is live run state which a dispatched agent must neither edit nor revert

title: A kill-check passes when any file in the suite catches the mutation, so a test file can free-ride on another's fixtures
description:
Every kill-check in this project runs the whole suite: mutate a production line, rebuild, and see whether ANY case goes red. That measures 'the suite catches this', which is the right property for the ratchet -- but it is routinely reported as evidence for 'test_X.cpp pins this behaviour', which is a different and stronger claim.

Found concretely in helios (ss-e5n). test_impshape.cpp is the file that names itself as the one testing impShape::setMatrix and impShape::invertMatrix. Its own fixtures were identity, pure-translation and diagonal matrices, so none of them could distinguish invmat's off-diagonal cofactor indices or tell setMatrix's transpose step from a verbatim copy. Those mutations still came back RED -- because test_imp_primitives.cpp's coupled-matrix fixtures were exercising setMatrix and invertMatrix through the primitives and catching them there.

The gap only became visible with a mutation that NOTHING in the suite caught: setPosition writing invmat[12] = -x * invmat[0] instead of -x. Every fixture in the file had invmat[0] == 1 exactly, so the factor was invisible. It survived until test_impshape.cpp was rebuilt on the coupled matrix.

Why it matters: a file whose discrimination comes entirely from another file's fixtures is one refactor away from silently becoming decoration. Deleting or weakening test_imp_primitives.cpp's coupled matrix would quietly un-pin invertMatrix, and nothing would report a coverage or kill-check regression, because test_impshape.cpp's own cases would still be green and still be counted.
design:
Two candidate mechanics, neither trivial:

1. Per-file kill-check: build and run only the cases from the file under test when checking its own mutations. The harness registers all TESTs into one binary, so this needs either a --filter argument on the driver (main.cpp already iterates a registry) or a per-file link. --filter by source file is the cheaper of the two.

2. Attribution rather than isolation: when a mutation goes RED, record WHICH cases failed, not just how many. That is already printed per-case by the harness. A kill-check that reports 'killed by test_imp_primitives.cpp, not by test_impshape.cpp' surfaces the free-riding without any build changes, and it is the same data the current sweeps already produce and discard.

(2) is the one to do first: it is a reporting change to the kill-check convention, costs nothing at build time, and would have caught this instance the moment the sweep was run.
acceptance_criteria: the kill-check convention used by test-writer and verifier records which file's cases failed, not only the count; a mutation of a function that file X claims to test, killed only by file Y, is reported as a finding rather than as a pass
notes:
RELATED FAILURE MODE, hit directly on 2026-08-22 during ss-or3's kill-check. Same class as this issue -- a kill-check reporting success while having proved nothing -- but one level further up, and cheaper to fix.

This issue is about attribution: the suite catches a mutation, so the check passes, but nothing says WHICH file caught it, so a test file can free-ride on another's fixtures.

The variant found here is worse, because it produces a false negative rather than a false positive. A mutation that matches nothing at all leaves the source unchanged, the suite passes, and the result is indistinguishable from a mutant the suite genuinely failed to kill. The natural reading of a green run is "coverage gap found" -- which is exactly the wrong conclusion, and the one nearly recorded.

Concretely: a mutant intended to weaken impCubeVolume's corner mask was written against 'cubes[index].value >= surfacevalue'. The real code reads 'cubes[index].value < surfacevalue' -- the >= form appears only in the crawl functions, on different variables. The substitution matched zero sites. The suite passed, and the first interpretation was that the tests could not see corner-mask changes. Re-run against the correct expression the mutant applied, still survived, and only THEN was it worth investigating -- at which point it turned out to be a genuine equivalent mutant (it moves 24 vertices and 48 zero-area triangles and leaves the triangulated area identical to six decimal places).

So the sequence was: broken mutant -> wrong conclusion -> corrected mutant -> right conclusion, and nothing in the process would have caught the first step.

The fix is one line in whatever runs the mutation: compare the file before and after, and fail loudly when it is unchanged. Cheaper than this issue's own fix and it removes an entire category of silently meaningless result. Worth doing in the same change, since both are about a kill-check that reports more confidence than it earned.

title: impShape::setMatrix discards invertMatrix's false, silently keeping a stale inverse
description:
Implicit/impShape.cpp's setMatrix calls invertMatrix() and ignores its bool return. invertMatrix returns false for a singular matrix and leaves invmat untouched -- so setMatrix then builds invtrmat from whatever inverse was there BEFORE, and every subsequent value() call silently transforms points with a stale matrix.

There is no error, no assert, and no way for a caller to find out. The shape simply keeps behaving as though it were still at its previous orientation.

Found by the independent /code-review of hyperspace PR #6 (ss-44s). It is NOT a defect introduced by that PR -- it is pre-existing production behaviour that the new setMatrix tests brought within sight without characterizing. tests/test_impshape.cpp covers invertMatrix's false return as a predicate (invertMatrix_returns_false_for_a_singular_matrix) but nothing covers what setMatrix does with it.

Whether this is a bug depends on a question only the project can answer: can a singular matrix reach setMatrix in the real screen saver? The callers are the implicit primitives, whose matrices come from quaternion rotations and translations and should never be singular. If that invariant holds this is dead defensive code and the right fix is an assert; if it does not, it is a silent-corruption path.

Shared core, so helios has the identical code and the identical gap.

Suggested next step: add a characterization test pinning the current stale-inverse behaviour first -- it is cheap and it makes whichever fix follows visible -- then decide between asserting and propagating.
acceptance_criteria: the current behaviour is characterized by a test, and the invariant question is answered in writing: either an assert with the reason, or a propagated failure with the callers updated

title: The marginal-gain floor compares against the previous log entry, which may be a different submodule
description:
/coverage-loop Stage 5 defines the floor as:

  'Compare this iteration's addressable against the previous entry's in
   .claude/artifacts/loop-log.json. Stop and escalate when the gain is below 1.0
   percentage point, or below a third of the previous iteration's gain.'

'The previous entry' is positional, not per-target. .claude/artifacts/loop-log.json is a single flat array across ALL submodules, so after the hyperspace run (ss-44s) it reads [helios/1, hyperspace/1]. Had hyperspace reached a second iteration, the rule would have compared hyperspace's gain against HELIOS' -- different code, different baseline, different denominator. The comparison is meaningless and the stop decision derived from it would be arbitrary.

It has not bitten yet only because both runs so far emptied their queue in iteration 1 and never reached the comparison.

FIX: select the previous entry with the same 'target', not the previous entry. If there is none, the floor does not apply -- which is the existing iteration-1 rule, and it then follows from the data instead of from the iteration number.

RELATED, and the reason this is worth filing rather than fixing silently: the floor rule has now failed to be exercised TWICE. ss-44s existed specifically to test it, chose hyperspace because a second iteration was thought likely, and the queue emptied in iteration 1 anyway -- as ss-44s's own NOTES predicted once the transitive pass re-triaged the twins. Two full runs in, the marginal-gain floor is still code that has never executed, and it now also has a known defect in the line that selects its comparand.

Both runs stopped on 'queue empty' with bucket A at zero uncovered regions. That is the loop working, but it means the floor cannot be exercised by running the loop as-is on a submodule whose queue fits in one iteration. Testing it needs either a target large enough to need two iterations, or a synthetic log fixture.
acceptance_criteria: the floor selects the previous entry for the same target; and the rule is exercised at least once, by a real two-iteration run or by a test against a synthetic loop-log fixture

title: impShape's destructor is non-virtual in hyperspace but virtual in helios
description:
hyperspace/Implicit/impShape.h:63 declares '~impShape(){};' where helios/Implicit/impShape.h:63 declares 'virtual ~impShape(){};'. Same shared C++ core, same line number, one word different.

impShape is the polymorphic base for every implicit primitive -- impCapsule, impEllipsoid, impKnot, impHexahedron, impRoundedHexahedron all derive from it. Deleting a derived shape through an impShape* in hyperspace runs only the base destructor; the derived one is skipped. That is undefined behaviour, and it leaks whatever the derived class owns.

Found by the triager during the hyperspace /coverage-loop run (ss-44s) while diffing the twins' ledgers. It is NOT a coverage problem and was deliberately not folded into the test work -- the destructors are bucket C ('empty body -- a test here exercises the compiler, not the code'), so no test in the wave touches this and no test would have caught it.

Which twin is right is the actual question. helios' virtual form is the safe one. Whether hyperspace diverged or helios was fixed is worth establishing before copying one onto the other, because it bears on ss-mws (whether the shared core stays duplicated) -- a core that has silently diverged on a correctness-relevant declaration is evidence for that decision.
acceptance_criteria: the divergence is resolved deliberately in whichever direction is correct, with the reason recorded; ss-mws notes it as evidence

title: Run /coverage-loop a second time, on hyperspace, to reach the marginal-gain floor
description:
ss-1gl ran the loop end to end for the first time and the machinery worked, but it could not exercise the one stage it most wanted to: the queue emptied in iteration 1, so the loop stopped on 'queue empty' and the marginal-gain floor never evaluated. That stop rule reads .claude/artifacts/loop-log.json, which now exists with exactly one entry -- so a second run is also the first test of the resume/compare path, which has never had a previous entry to compare against.

hyperspace is the right target. It is helios' twin: the identical shared C++ core, the same 214-entry ledger, and a baseline that still reads 496/2374 because it received none of helios' tests. So the queue is already understood, the expected gain is known within a few points, and any divergence between the twins is itself information.

Do ss-1sp first. Running another wave of submodule commits through a guard that checks the wrong repository would repeat the same unprotected run knowingly.
acceptance_criteria: a second loop-log entry exists; the floor rule is evaluated against a real previous iteration and its decision recorded, whether it stops the loop or not
notes:
RUN COMPLETE THROUGH STAGE 5; NOT MERGED. hyperspace PR #6 is open with CI
green and both review passes addressed. The merge was declined when offered, so
it is left for the user; the superproject side is deliberately uncommitted
behind it (see below).

RESULT: 20.89% -> 63.59% lines (496/2374 -> 1507/2370), 49 -> 160 cases, 11
commits, every line under tests/. Bucket A finished at ZERO uncovered regions.
The twins now agree to the region: both 123 A / 455, 23 B / 525, 68 C / 77, both
capped at 455/980 = 46.4% by ss-aio.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERION NOT MET. This issue asked for the marginal-gain floor to be
"evaluated against a real previous iteration and its decision recorded". It was
not, and could not be: the queue emptied in iteration 1 again, exactly as this
issue's own NOTES predicted once the transitive pass re-triaged the twins. Two
runs in, the floor remains code that has never executed.

Worse, the run found a defect IN the floor rule that would have made a second
iteration's decision meaningless anyway: it compares against "the previous
entry" in a log that is a flat array across all submodules, so hyperspace
iteration 2 would have been compared against HELIOS iteration 1. Filed as ss-j5z,
which also carries the "exercise it at least once" requirement forward. Do not
close this issue as satisfied; ss-j5z is where the remaining work lives.

WHY THE SUPERPROJECT IS UNCOMMITTED: coverage/hyperspace.baseline.json (63.59%)
and coverage/hyperspace.triage.json are regenerated on disk, and the hyperspace
gitlink points at 803289a. That commit is not on hyperspace master until PR #6
merges, and bumping to it first is exactly what CLAUDE.md forbids -- it pins the
superproject to a SHA that can vanish. The raised baseline cannot land without
the pointer either, or the gate fails for anyone whose submodule is still at the
old commit. So all three move together, after the merge.

REMAINING, in order:
  1. gh pr merge 6 --squash --delete-branch   (in hyperspace)
  2. take the MERGE COMMIT sha, not the branch tip -- squash rewrites it
  3. in the superproject on test/coverage-hyperspace, stage BY PATH:
     the hyperspace gitlink, coverage/hyperspace.baseline.json,

     concurrent session's notes/ rule that is not part of this work.
  4. push, PR, review, merge
  5. git -C hyperspace switch master && git -C hyperspace pull --ff-only

     detached blocks the next one

Run complete and merged (hyperspace#6 -> ac09a83, screen-savers#30 -> 55dfec1). The coverage half succeeded well beyond expectation; the half this issue was actually created for did not, and cannot be satisfied by re-running the loop on hyperspace.

NOT DELIVERED: the second clause -- 'the floor rule is evaluated against a real previous iteration and its decision recorded'. The queue emptied in iteration 1 again, exactly as this issue's own NOTES predicted, so the floor never ran. Closing rather than leaving open because no action taken against THIS issue can now satisfy it. ss-j5z owns the remainder and states it directly: fix the rule to select the previous entry for the same target, and exercise it at least once -- by a target large enough to need two iterations, or a synthetic loop-log fixture. The synthetic-fixture option is the realistic one; both submodules that have run the loop finished in a single iteration.

The run's real yield was elsewhere, and is worth recording as the reason it was not wasted: twenty undiscriminating test paths were found and fixed, ten inherited from helios and ten created fresh in this wave, every one of which had passed its author's own kill-check. ss-1sp was confirmed fixed in the field and ss-jl7 shown to have recurred worse. ss-p45 was reproduced independently on a second submodule. title: The addressable ceiling mixes units and keeps unreachable regions in its denominator
description:
Two defects in the loop's own success metric, both found by running it (ss-1gl).

1. UNREACHABLE DENOMINATOR. addressable = covered / (all regions - C regions). Bucket B stays in the denominator, but B is by definition the work that cannot be done until something is refactored. On helios, ss-aio's 525 B regions are 53% of the 980-region denominator and are blocked on an open project decision, so covering every single queued entry could not have exceeded ~48%. The loop's default threshold of 80 was unreachable before the run started, and nothing said so -- Stage 2 is supposed to stop early if the ceiling already meets the threshold, but there is no check for a threshold the ceiling cannot reach.

2. UNIT MISMATCH. /coverage-loop Stage 5 says addressable is 'that coverage over the denominator in this iteration's triage ledger'. But the gate measures LINES (helios finished at 1506/2370) and the ledger counts llvm-cov REGIONS (507/980). Dividing one by the other is meaningless. The figures in the first run's loop log came from re-running the classifier instead, which is a full extra pass the spec does not budget for.

Fix directions for 1: report the reachable ceiling alongside the addressable one, and refuse a threshold above it at Stage 0 rather than discovering it at Stage 5. For 2: either have the gate report regions, or define addressable in line terms, or have Stage 2 return both numbers so Stage 5 never has to divide across metrics.
acceptance_criteria: a run whose threshold exceeds the reachable ceiling says so at Stage 0; addressable is computed from one metric end to end, with no reclassification pass needed to obtain it
notes:
NEW EVIDENCE 2026-08-21, from the ss-aio fix. The metric is not a ceiling at all.

triage_classify.py:428-439 is the whole formula:

    addressable = total - regions["C"]
    ceiling = 100.0 * covered_regions / addressable

So it is current coverage over a denominator that drops C. It never reads the A/B split, which means the one question triage exists to answer -- how much work is available right now -- is the one thing this number cannot express.

Demonstrated by running it either side of the ss-aio reconciliation, same working tree, coverage untouched between the two runs:

              bucket A            bucket B            printed ceiling
  before      124 fn / 456 rg     22 fn / 526 rg      55.0% of 982
  after       140 fn / 934 rg      6 fn /  48 rg      55.0% of 982

478 regions moved from unreachable to reachable and the number did not twitch. Bucket B is still sitting in the denominator while being unreachable by definition, which is exactly what this issue already says -- this is just the first time the two have been observed side by side with everything else held constant.

The other half is the name. A ceiling is what coverage could reach; this is what coverage has reached. It moved 46.4% -> 55.0% across the ss-aio work purely because covered_regions grew, which is the giveaway: a ceiling does not rise when you write a test, it rises when you unblock one.

The figure that would have been worth printing at both those rows is A-bucket completion -- 100% before (bucket A had 0 uncovered regions, which is why the loop stopped), and a much lower number after, because 478 newly-reachable regions arrived uncovered. That is the number that tells a reader whether to run the loop again, and both coverage-loop runs recorded their stop decisions against the one that cannot.

title: Close the nine undiscriminating paths and the stale comments in the helios test wave
description:
Stage 5 of the first /coverage-loop run (ss-1gl) returned pass-with-findings. The wave is sound -- 2169 insertions, all under tests/, no production source touched, and every commit contains tests that genuinely kill mutations. But four paths inside otherwise-real tests do not discriminate, and each survived the writer's own kill-check. Each fix is a few lines.

1. MEDIUM tests/test_rsmath_free.cpp:180,188 -- cosf/sinf sample only exact multiples of pi/2, where rsCosf's table fraction is always zero. Deleting the whole interpolation term leaves the suite green, as does multiplying it by 7 or doubling the fraction scale. The test comment claims it catches a dropped fraction term; it does not. Fix: one sample off a table boundary, e.g. rsCosf(0.31f) vs cosf(0.31f), where the un-interpolated error is ~2e-3.

2. MEDIUM tests/test_cubetables.cpp:212,225 -- operator< and operator> are not distinguished from index ordering, because the fixture uses sortableCube(0) and sortableCube(1), whose indices sort the same way as their depths. Rewriting the operators to compare .index leaves the suite green. This is precisely the swap the commit message claims to prevent. The == and != cases are safe (indices 3 and 9). Fix: invert the indices, e.g. near_cube(9), far_cube(1).

3. MEDIUM tests/test_impknot.cpp:84,108,123,137 -- the twists -> twistsOverCoils -> lat path in impKnot::value is unexercised. Every fixture is a point on the x axis, so rsAtan2f(ty,tx) is 0 and lat is 0 whatever twistsOverCoils holds. Replacing the production line with const float lat(0.0f) leaves the suite green, as does changing twistsf/coilsf to twistsf*coilsf. Fix: one value() case off-axis at two different setNumTwists settings, asserting they differ.

4. LOW tests/test_imp_primitives.cpp:304-338 -- impRoundedHexahedron's width/height/length all default to 1.0 and no test changes them, so which parameter an axis reads is invisible; swapping length for width in the zz term leaves the suite green. Fix: set distinct extents before the pastAll case.

Verifier's own conclusion: none of these justifies rejecting the wave. They are follow-ups, and they are worth doing because each one is a test that currently claims coverage it does not provide.
acceptance_criteria: each of the nine mutations named in the description and notes fails the suite; the fixes are committed in the submodule with the same kill-check standard as the wave, and the stale 'no bd issue filed yet' comments at test_rsmath.cpp:646 and :783 name ss-c6g and ss-9wk
notes:
TENTH PATH, found during the hyperspace run (ss-44s) and still present in helios.

helios/tests/test_rsvec4.cpp's transPoint/transVec fixtures use point(1,1,1,1) and
direction(1,1,1,99). Because y == z, the m[4] and m[8] terms carry equal
coefficients, so swapping those two matrix columns in the production source is
invisible. The hyperspace writer hit it by copying the fixture structurally,
ran the m[4]/m[8] swap as its kill-check, and got GREEN.

Fixed in hyperspace before commit by switching to point(1,2,3,4) /
direction(1,2,3,99) and recomputing the expected outputs; the same swap then
fails as it should. hyperspace/tests/test_rsvec4.cpp (5b7705e) has the corrected
form.

Same root cause as items 3, 4 and 9: a fixture whose components cannot
distinguish the indices the test claims to pin. It was not caught by the
original verifier because test_rsvec4.cpp was not among the files it flagged --
which is itself worth noting, since it means the nine were a sample rather than
an exhaustive sweep.

So the fix list for helios is ten paths, not nine, and the general remedy is the
same one item 9 already names: fixtures with distinct, non-trivial components.

--- RESOLUTION (helios PR #8, branch test/fix-undiscriminating-paths) ---

All ten fixed, in seven commits, every line under tests/. Production tree
hashes for Implicit/, rsMath/, Rgbhsl/ and util/ are byte-identical to the
branch point. 158 -> 169 cases. Gate: lines 63.6%, baseline 63.5%, PASS.

THREE MORE OF THE SAME CLASS were found while proving the fixes, by running
mutations rather than by reading:

  A  impCapsule's tx row could read the ty row's invtrmat entries
  B  impKnot::addCrawlPoint  mat[8] -> mat[4]   (identity fixture, both zero)
  C/D impTorus::center and ::addCrawlPoint  mat[1] -> mat[4]  (same)
  E/F impShape::setPosition  invmat[12] = -x * invmat[0], and the invtrmat
      equivalent -- invisible wherever the matrix is identity, since both
      factors are exactly 1 there

E and F matter beyond helios: they were NOT among the ten, and hyperspace
only catches them because its setPosition test was rebuilt on the coupled
matrix. The lesson is that "the suite kills this mutation" and "the file
that claims to test this kills this mutation" are different properties, and
only the first one gets measured. test_impshape.cpp's own fixtures did not
discriminate; test_imp_primitives.cpp's coupled matrix was doing the work.

All thirteen were GREEN at the branch point and RED at HEAD. Full table in
the PR body and per-commit in each message.

Two deliberate divergences from hyperspace's corrected files, both keeping a
case hyperspace dropped: roundedHexahedron_value_sums_all_three_axes_past_the_box
(re-derived against the new distinct extents -- every other case clears
exactly one extent, so nothing else shows the three clamped terms summing),
and the pi/2 boundary samples in test_rsmath_free.cpp (kept alongside the new
mid-bucket ones; they still pin the scale constant and the table choice).

Also fixed, same class, not among the ten: test_rsmath.cpp's
matrix_rotationInvert_does_not_actually_invert_the_rotation described two
cases and built one, and passed rsVec(1,2,2) -- length 3 -- to make(), which
documents a NORMALIZED axis. toMat divides by the norm squared so the matrix
came out orthonormal and the test passed, but the rotation was not by 0.9 rad.
Both cases are built now and the axis is normalized. This is a
correctness-of-claim fix, not a new kill: the generic case alone already
killed the cofactor mutations.

title: Two of eight submodule commits produced no guard record at all
description:
During the first /coverage-loop run (ss-1gl), helios received 8 test commits. .claude/artifacts/hook-log.jsonl holds only 6 guard-default-branch allow records for them.

Commits at 21:06:54Z (4f41b43) and 21:29:18Z (a11858a) have no allow. The nearest records either side are 'skip | no git commit or push in command' at 21:06:52/21:06:58 and 21:29:17/21:29:20 -- so the hook was running, and either it did not see those commands or it did not recognise them as commits.

I could not reproduce it. Probes of the obvious candidates all parse correctly and return allow: heredoc via 'git commit -q -F - <<MSG', an apostrophe inside a double-quoted -m, and 'cd helios && git commit'. So the cause is not established, which is the reason to file rather than guess.

This is what the loop log's guards block exists to catch. /coverage-loop Stage 5 says all-zero counts for a hook that should have fired are a finding, not a clean run -- the same logic applies to a count that is short. Both hooks fail open on their own bugs, so a guard that silently skips a commit is indistinguishable from a clean one without this arithmetic.

Depends on ss-53x's sibling finding only in spirit; the concrete blocker is that hook-log.jsonl records decisions but not the command that produced them, so a skip cannot be traced back to its input.
acceptance_criteria: either the two commits' skip is reproduced and fixed, or hook-log.jsonl records enough of the command to make the next occurrence diagnosable
notes:
RECURRED IN THE HYPERSPACE RUN (ss-44s), at a HIGHER rate: 4 of 9 commits
produced no guard record, against 2 of 8 in helios. Across both runs that is
6 of 17 submodule commits with no hook decision logged at all.

Matched by timestamp, hyperspace commits (UTC) against guard-default-branch
'allow' rows in .claude/artifacts/hook-log.jsonl:

  17fe044  23:58:52  test: cover rsMatrix and rsQuat's wider transform...   NO RECORD
  9497bd1  00:08:01  test: cover the implicit primitives' value()...        NO RECORD
  5b7705e  00:13:29  test: cover rsVec4 arithmetic, transforms...           allow
  51ac311  00:19:17  test: cover hslTween, rgbTween...                      NO RECORD
  3ba5d67  00:27:47  test: cover impKnot's value/center/addCrawlPoint...    allow
  d4293e3  00:35:44  test: cover impShape's construction...                 allow
  17dc77b  00:40:20  test: cover sortableCube ordering...                   allow
  b535b19  00:42:19  test: cover rsSqrtf, rsInvSqrtf...                     allow
  667f41d  01:10:57  test: fix undiscriminating fromEuler...                NO RECORD

The five that DID record read 'commit in hyperspace on test/coverage-loop' --
the correct repository and the correct branch. So ss-1sp's fix is confirmed
working in the field: helios' run logged 'commit in screen-savers on
test/coverage-helios' for the same shape of command. That is the good news, and
it is what makes this issue the remaining gap rather than a duplicate of it.

WHAT THIS RULES OUT: it is not the cd-resolution bug. Those five prove the hook
resolves a submodule commit correctly when it runs at all. The four misses are
the hook NOT RUNNING, or running and not logging -- a different failure.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE COUNT SUGGESTS: both hooks fail open by design, so
a hook that has silently stopped firing is indistinguishable from a clean run.
Stage 5 of /coverage-loop uses these counts as the ONLY signal that the guard is
alive -- 'All-zero counts for a hook that should have fired are a finding, not a
clean run.' A 5-of-9 count passes that check while 44% of the wave went
unguarded. The check as written cannot detect partial silence, only total
silence.

No pattern is obvious in the four: they are not the first commit, not one
agent's, not one file's, and not clustered in time. Two were the first commit of
their dispatch and two were not.

NEXT STEP SUGGESTION: the loop should reconcile commits against guard records
directly -- count commits on the branch since the branch point and require a
matching allow for each -- rather than checking the decision count is nonzero.
That turns this from something spotted by hand into something Stage 5 fails on.

title: coverage-runner wrote three files into the helios working tree
description:
During Stage 1 of the first /coverage-loop run (ss-1gl), the coverage-runner agent -- specified as read-only, 'it measures, it never edits' -- left helios/helios.json, helios/hills.json and helios/hyperspace.json as untracked files inside the submodule working tree. It reported this itself and said its own rm was blocked by the permission classifier.

This is ss-ke7 demonstrating itself on the loop's very first run: instructed restraint is not restraint. The agent holds Bash, a shell redirect is Bash, and the only thing that stopped the cleanup was a classifier the agent did not expect.

It is also the exact Stage 0 hazard the loop documents. Untracked files inside a submodule make the *superproject* report ' M helios' and nothing else, which is why Stage 0 step 1 insists on --ignore-submodules=untracked. Had the next run started before someone noticed, it would have stopped citing the wrong repository.

Cleaned up by hand this run (the files were plainly generated coverage reports; verified by content before deleting). Filed with the coverage-loop-blocked label so Stage 0 step 6 counts it.

Underlying cause is filed separately as ss-ke7 -- this is the evidence for it, not a duplicate.
acceptance_criteria: a coverage-runner dispatch cannot create a file anywhere in the repo; demonstrated by attempting the same --json invocation under the restricted tool set

title: tools/ has no test harness, so its Python is verified by hand or not at all
description:
tools/triage_classify.py, tools/coverage_regions.py and tools/coverage_report.py have no tests. The ss-dgw fix was verified with a throwaway driver in a job tmp dir, run once against the patched and unpatched functions, and then discarded -- the kill-check happened but left no artifact anyone can re-run.

This is the same exposure as ss-b4a from the other side: ss-b4a triangulates the region *measurement* against a hand-counted fixture, this covers the ledger logic sitting on top of it. Both exist because doctrine treats tools/ as axiomatic, so a bug in it is inherited by every verdict and every gate result downstream.

Smallest useful shape: tools/tests/ with plain unittest, no new dependency, runnable as python3 -m unittest discover. Seed it with the four set_verdict cases from the ss-dgw fix, all four of which fail against the pre-fix function.
acceptance_criteria: tools/tests/ exists, runs with a single documented command, and contains at least the six set_verdict regression cases from the ss-dgw fix -- including confirm-then-change and the round trip through the rule's verdict, which fail against the first patch as well as the pre-fix code

title: triage --set leaves the ledger's counts block stale
description:
tools/triage_classify.py set_verdict() rewrites a single entry's verdict and writes the ledger back without recomputing data['counts']. The counts block is therefore only correct until the first --set, and stays wrong until someone happens to run a full triage.

Already drifted in the tree: coverage/hyperspace.triage.json reports 144 testable / 3 needs-refactoring while its entries are 143 A / 4 B. helios agrees with its entries only because it got a full re-triage after the same --set.

This matters now because ss-aio's transitive-coupling verdicts need seven more --set calls per twin. Fourteen sets against a function that never recomputes would leave the summary eight functions wrong in both ledgers -- and the counts block is what the triager and /coverage-loop Stage 2 report as the bucket split.
acceptance_criteria: set_verdict recomputes counts from the ledger's entries before writing; both twins' counts agree with their entries
close_reason: Fixed and merged in dcef957 (PR #22): set_verdict now recomputes counts from the ledger's non-stale entries. Verified both twins agree with their entries -- helios and hyperspace each report 124 A / 23 B / 67 C in counts and hold 124 A / 23 B / 67 C in entries.

title: Close the gap where a submodule PR cannot be verified in its own repo
description: coverage.sh, the configs and the baselines all live in the superproject. A submodule PR merges first, reviewed by someone who cannot run the gate and cannot see the baseline change; the superproject PR carrying the measurement lands after the code it measures is already on master. tests.yml narrows this to a smoke test but cannot close it.
