title: The two-argument makeSurface clamps out-of-volume crawl points to the wrong face
description:
impCubeVolume::makeSurface(impCrawlPointVector&) declares its grid indices as 'unsigned int i, j, k' (impCubeVolume.cpp:183) and then clamps them as if they were signed:

    i = int((cpv[cp].position[0] - lbf[0]) / cubewidth);
    if(i < 0)        i = 0;
    if(i >= int(w))  i = int(w) - 1;

Two consequences, both from the declared type:

1. 'if(i < 0)' is unreachable. An unsigned int is never negative, and the
   compiler folds the branch away.
2. 'i >= int(w)' promotes int(w) to unsigned for the comparison, so the huge
   value a negative result wrapped to passes it.

So a crawl point to the left of the volume clamps to w-1 -- the +x face -- instead of 0, the -x face. Worked example with the test suite's geometry (16 cubes at width 0.25, lbf[0] = -2): a crawl point at x = -10 computes int(-32), which becomes 4294967264 as unsigned, compares >= 16, and clamps to 15. The crawl then starts on the opposite side of the volume from the point that asked for it.

THE FOUR-ARGUMENT OVERLOAD GETS THIS RIGHT. makeSurface(float, float, float, impCrawlPointVector&) at impCubeVolume.cpp:351 declares 'int i, j, k' with the identical clamp below it. Same author, same block, same intent -- which is what makes this a typo in one overload rather than a deliberate choice in both.

Impact in the savers is probably nil: Helios.cpp seeds crawl points from the metaball centres, which are inside the volume by construction. It matters because the clamp exists precisely to make out-of-volume seeds safe, and it silently does the opposite of what it says. Anything that starts feeding it externally-derived positions inherits a bug that looks like it was already handled.

Not covered by ss-or3's suite, which keeps its sphere and its seeds well clear of the boundary on purpose. ss-c49 is the issue that extends crawl coverage and is the natural place to add a case that pins the clamp -- a seed outside the volume on the -x side should crawl the same surface as one just inside it.

Found by the independent review pass on helios#10 / hyperspace#8. Identical in both twins.

## Steps to Reproduce

Call makeSurface(cpv) with a single crawl point whose x is well left of lbf[0]. Instrument or step the clamp: i arrives at w-1 rather than 0.

## Acceptance Criteria

Both overloads clamp out-of-volume crawl points to the nearest face, the signed/unsigned mismatch is gone, and a test pins it in both twins.

title: impCubeVolume's destructor never deletes the impSurface its constructor allocates
description:
impCubeVolume::impCubeVolume() does 'surface = new impSurface' (impCubeVolume.cpp:40). ~impCubeVolume() clears its three vectors and returns. Nothing anywhere in either twin calls delete on that pointer -- grep for 'delete surface' finds nothing in impCubeVolume.cpp or .h.

MEASURED, not inferred. A program constructing three impCubeVolumes and letting each fall out of scope:

  $ leaks --atExit -- ./leak2
  Process: 3 leaks for 480 total leaked bytes.

Three constructions, three leaks, 160 bytes each -- the size of an impSurface.

Pre-existing, and identical in helios and hyperspace. It has been invisible until now for a reason worth stating: the savers construct their volumes once at startup and run until the process dies, so a per-process leak of one object never mattered. Nothing had ever constructed an impCubeVolume in a loop, because until ss-aio nothing could construct one at all outside a renderer.

Why this is filed rather than fixed in the ss-aio PR:

The fix is not one line, because ownership is genuinely ambiguous. setSurface(impSurface*) is public and lets a caller install a surface impCubeVolume did not allocate. A bare 'delete surface' in the destructor would double-free for any caller doing that, and getSurface() hands the raw pointer out as well. Doing it properly means deciding whether impCubeVolume owns its surface -- a std::unique_ptr and a setSurface taking ownership, or a bool tracking whether it allocated the one it holds. That is a design call on a class the Metal port is about to rewrite, and it is outside what ss-aio was scoped to do.

Why it will stop being harmless:

ss-or3 characterizes impCubeVolume, which means many constructions per test run rather than one per process. And the moment anyone adds -fsanitize=address or -fsanitize=leak to the coverage build's instrument flags -- a reasonable thing to want once this code is testable -- the suite starts failing on it. Better to have decided before then.

Found by the independent review pass on the ss-aio PRs, not by the author.

## Steps to Reproduce

Compile a main() that constructs three impCubeVolumes in a loop against Implicit/ and rsMath/, link -framework OpenGL, and run under 'leaks --atExit'. Reports 3 leaks / 480 bytes. Requires the ss-aio fix to be present, since before it the program cannot get past the first constructor.

## Acceptance Criteria

impCubeVolume has a stated ownership rule for its surface, that rule is enforced by the type or by the destructor, and constructing and destroying impCubeVolumes in a loop leaks nothing. Both twins.

title: rsMatrix::preMult and postMult are tested only with a translation and a uniform scale, so their operand snapshot's indices are unpinned
description:
Same defect class as ss-e5n, in a file the same wave wrote, found by mutation while proving ss-e5n's fixes in helios. Not fixed there -- ss-e5n's scope was the ten named paths, and this is an eleventh in a different file.

helios/tests/test_rsmath.cpp:510 and :529 are the only tests that call rsMatrix::preMult or postMult directly. Both build the same two operands: t.makeTranslate(5,0,0) and s.makeScale(2,2,2). A translation's linear part is the identity and a uniform scale's is diagonal, so every off-diagonal entry of both operands is exactly zero and every diagonal entry of one of them is exactly 1.

preMult opens by snapshotting all sixteen entries of *this into preMat0..preMat15 before overwriting them. Swapping which entry two of those locals read -- preMat1 taking m[4] and preMat4 taking m[1], a transpose confined to the linear block -- leaves the suite GREEN. Both are 0 in every fixture, so the swap has nothing to change.

Verified against helios at test/fix-undiscriminating-paths (169 cases):
  const float preMat1(m[1]) <-> const float preMat4(m[4])   0 failed, GREEN

The two tests do discriminate what they claim to: the 10-vs-5 translation assertion flips under a preMult/postMult swap, which is what their comments say they are for. The gap is narrower -- the composition ORDER is pinned, the operand INDEXING is not.
design:
The remedy ss-e5n established: a fixture whose components are distinct and non-trivial. Compose two matrices with fully populated, non-symmetric linear parts instead of a translation and a uniform scale, and assert the full product. The coupled matrix already used by helios' and hyperspace's Implicit tests ([[2,1.5,-1.5],[1,3,1],[1,1,4]] column-major, translation (1,2,3)) is a ready-made non-symmetric operand; a second, different one is needed for the other side, since M*M cannot distinguish M from its transpose in every entry.

Keep the existing 10-vs-5 cases -- they state the order property sharply and a full-product assertion states it less legibly.
acceptance_criteria: a preMat_i/preMat_j swap confined to preMult's linear block fails the suite; the same for postMult's snapshot; the existing 10-vs-5 order assertions still present

title: Backport two dropped cases from helios' test wave to hyperspace
description:
When ss-e5n's fixes were ported from hyperspace to helios, two cases were kept in helios that hyperspace's corrected files had dropped. Both are real coverage of behaviour nothing else in either suite states, so hyperspace is the one that is now short.

1. roundedHexahedron_value_sums_all_three_axes_past_the_box. hyperspace replaced it with roundedHexahedron_value_only_the_axis_past_its_own_extent_contributes, whose three cases each clear exactly ONE extent. Nothing left in hyperspace shows sx, sy and sz all unclamped and summing -- which is the whole shape of the formula. helios kept it, re-derived against the new distinct extents (1,2,3): point (2,3,4) clears each extent by 1, so the sum is 3.

2. The pi/2 boundary samples in cosf/sinf. ss-e5n item 1 was that sampling ONLY at multiples of pi/2 leaves the interpolation fraction at zero, so the fraction term is unpinned. The fix is a mid-bucket sample -- but hyperspace removed the boundary cases when it added them. Those cases still pin the scale constant and the choice of table, which the mid-bucket samples state less sharply (a mid-bucket sample compared against cosf catches everything, but when it fails it does not say which of the four failure modes it was). helios kept both.

Neither is urgent -- in both cases hyperspace's remaining tests are discriminating, just less specific. This is a small port in the opposite direction from the usual one.
acceptance_criteria: hyperspace/tests/test_imp_primitives.cpp has a case where all three roundedHexahedron extents are cleared at once; hyperspace/tests/test_rsmath_free.cpp checks the pi/2 boundaries alongside its mid-bucket samples; both proven by the same kill-check standard

title: Stage 3's post-dispatch cleanliness check never looks at the superproject
description:
NOTE: this issue was filed on evidence that turned out to be wrong. Corrected below; the residual gap is real but theoretical, and no instance of it has been observed.

WHAT WAS ORIGINALLY CLAIMED: that a test-writer in the hyperspace run (ss-44s) added 'notes/' to the superproject's .gitignore, twice, without reporting it.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED: the user was running a SECOND, concurrent Claude session in the same working directory, writing an outside review into notes/. That session added the .gitignore rule -- correctly, and with a reasoned comment -- and then wrote notes/chap-improvements.md. The orchestrator of this run saw an unexplained .gitignore diff, assumed a subagent had made it, and reverted it twice, clobbering the other session's change. It was restored once notes/chap-improvements.md surfaced and the user confirmed it.

No test-writer mutated the superproject in this run. All four reported their superproject observations accurately.

THE RESIDUAL, THEORETICAL GAP: /coverage-loop Stage 3 still says only

  'Check git -C <submodule> status --short after each one and stop the loop if
   it is not clean.'

which reads the submodule tree alone. A writer that edited coverage/<name>.json, a *.baseline.json, or the superproject tooling would pass that check, and the standing rule forbidding exactly those edits would not be enforced until the verifier ran at Stage 5, a full wave later. That is worth closing, but it is a hardening task on an unexercised path, not a response to an observed defect -- hence P3, and the coverage-loop-blocked label removed so it does not count against Stage 0's escalation budget.

A SECOND, REAL LESSON, which is the more valuable half: the loop has no concept of a concurrent session sharing its working directory. This run switched the superproject's branch (main -> test/coverage-hyperspace) under another session that was actively working in the same checkout, and then twice reverted a file that session had edited. Stage 0's preflight treats a dirty tree as 'work in progress that the loop's commits and resets would destroy' and stops -- but it only looks once, at the start, so anything the other session does mid-run is invisible to it and looks exactly like a misbehaving subagent. An unexplained superproject diff appearing mid-run is at least as likely to be a human or another agent as it is to be a defect, and the loop currently has no way to tell those apart and no instruction to ask.
acceptance_criteria: Stage 3 checks both trees with the documented exceptions; and Stage 0 or Stage 3 says what to do when an unexplained superproject change appears mid-run, rather than leaving the orchestrator to guess and revert
notes:
RECURRED, and the second instance is worse than the first.

After the orchestrator reverted the first 'notes/' .gitignore entry, a later
writer in the same run re-added it -- with a FULLER comment than the original:

    # Scratch notes -- outside reads, drafts, working thinking. Deliberately not
    # tracked: docs/ is the knowledge base, and anything worth keeping graduates
    # into it as a lesson or a reference document.
    notes/

Two things this establishes that one instance did not:

1. It is CONVERGENT, not a slip. Two independent agents, given different files
   to test, both decided this repo should ignore notes/ and both wrote a
   rationale in the project's own voice. Nothing instructs it: grep over
   .claude/, docs/, CLAUDE.md and the installed skills finds no reference to a
   notes/ directory. So the behaviour will keep recurring and a one-time revert
   is not a fix.

2. It is MISREPORTED. The second writer's own status report described
   .gitignore as an 'unrelated pre-existing modification ... from outside this
   turn'. It was not pre-existing -- the orchestrator had reverted it to clean
   before that dispatch started. The agent did not know it had made the edit.

That second point is the reason this cannot be handled by asking writers to
report what they touched: the report was made in good faith and was wrong.
Only a diff of the superproject across the dispatch catches it, which is what
this issue asks Stage 3 to do.

No notes/ directory ever existed on disk in either instance -- the ignore rule
was added for scratch space that was created and removed, or never created.

title: Stage 0's clean-tree rule forbids exactly what Stage 0 step 5 creates
description:
/coverage-loop Stage 0 step 1 stops the run on any dirty file outside coverage/*.triage.json and coverage/*.baseline.json. Step 5 of the same stage says to claim or file a bd issue for the run -- and bd rewrites .beads/issues.jsonl on every create, claim and close.

So a strict reading of Stage 0 stops every run at its own step 5, and any bd activity during the run re-dirties the tree that Stage 1 onwards expects to be clean. In the first run (ss-1gl) this surfaced immediately: closing ss-dgw and filing two issues left .beads/*.jsonl modified before Stage 0 had finished, and each of the ten issues filed mid-run dirtied it again.

Worked around by committing the tracker state onto the loop's own branch before Stage 1, which is honest but undocumented and unobvious.

Fix: add .beads/ to the exemption list Stage 0 already keeps for the coverage artifacts, and say why -- the tracker is the loop's own bookkeeping, not work in progress that a reset would destroy.
acceptance_criteria: Stage 0's exemption list covers the tracker, or step 5 is explicit about committing it first; a run that files a bd issue no longer trips its own preflight

title: rsMatrix::rotationInvert reproduces its input instead of inverting it
description:
Found while writing characterization tests in the first /coverage-loop run (ss-1gl). rsMatrix::rotationInvert returns the input rotation matrix rather than its inverse. Confirmed for both an axis-aligned quarter turn and a generic-axis rotation.

For a pure rotation the inverse is the transpose, so the intended one-line implementation is a transpose of the 3x3 block; whatever it does now is not that. Any caller relying on it is getting a rotation applied twice in the same direction rather than undone.

Locked in by matrix_rotationInvert_does_not_actually_invert_the_rotation in helios tests/test_rsmath.cpp, which asserts the current wrong behaviour. Fixing the function means updating that test in the same change -- that is the intended workflow, not a conflict.

The shared C++ core is duplicated, so hyperspace carries the identical defect. Worth checking whether anything in either saver actually calls it before deciding between fixing and deleting.
acceptance_criteria: rotationInvert returns the inverse rotation, verified against composing it with its source to the identity; the characterization test is updated to the correct behaviour and the twin in hyperspace with it

title: rsQuat::fromMat's trace<=0 branch has two defects beyond the slerp bug
description:
Found while writing characterization tests in the first /coverage-loop run (ss-1gl). Both defects are now locked in by tests in helios tests/test_rsmath.cpp, which assert the wrong-but-current behaviour so the Metal port cannot change it silently.

1. The dominant axis component is read from whatever the caller's quaternion already held: the code does q[i] *= 0.5f where the algebra needs q[i] = b * 0.5f. So fromMat's output depends on the prior contents of the destination quaternion, which is the same class of defect as ss-qss.

2. The two non-dominant components pull the wrong matrix entries -- a difference where the algebra needs a sum.

Only the trace>0 path is correct, which is why this went unnoticed: it is the branch a well-conditioned rotation usually takes.

Same conversion family as ss-qss and headed for the same rewrite, so it should be decided alongside it rather than patched in isolation. The shared C++ core is duplicated, so hyperspace carries the identical defect.

Characterizing tests: quat_fromMat_dominant_axis_branches_zero_the_axis_component_on_a_fresh_quat, quat_fromMat_dominant_axis_component_is_read_from_whatever_the_caller_left_there, quat_fromMat_off_axis_dominant_branch_also_miscomputes_the_other_two_components.
acceptance_criteria: fromMat's trace<=0 branch produces a quaternion independent of the destination's prior contents and matching the trace>0 path on the same rotation; the characterization tests are updated in the same change and the twin in hyperspace with them

title: coverage.sh --json takes a directory, so --json helios silently runs all three submodules
description:
tools/coverage.sh --json <arg> treats <arg> as the output DIRECTORY, not a submodule filter. So './tools/coverage.sh --json helios' runs all three submodules and writes helios.json, hills.json and hyperspace.json into a directory named 'helios' -- which, run from the repo root, is the helios submodule's working tree.

Found when the Stage 1 coverage-runner did exactly this on the first loop run and left three untracked files in the submodule (see the sibling issue).

The positional-submodule form is './tools/coverage.sh helios', so the two spellings differ by a flag and mean entirely different things, with no error for the confusing one. Options: reject a --json target that is an existing submodule directory, require --json-dir for the directory sense, or refuse to write reports inside a submodule working tree.
acceptance_criteria: the confusing invocation either errors or cannot write into a submodule working tree
notes: Recurred within the same run. After the stray files were cleaned up by hand at Stage 1, a later Stage 3 test-writer found the same three files (helios.json, hills.json, hyperspace.json) back in the helios working tree and removed them again before it could commit. So this is not a one-off mistake by one agent -- the confusing invocation is reachable enough that two separate agents hit it in a single loop run, and each time it silently plants untracked files inside a submodule. Raises the priority case for rejecting the invocation outright rather than documenting it.

title: hyperspace's ledger carries a rule_would_say the rules cannot have produced
description:
coverage/hyperspace.triage.json records impCubeVolume::polygonize(unsigned int) with rule_would_say {verdict: A, rule: unknown:span}. unknown:span (triage_classify.py:337) returns '?' and nothing else, so no run of the classifier produced that pair. helios' copy of the same function correctly says {verdict: '?', rule: unknown:span}.

It is the fingerprint of ss-dgw: a human's earlier A relabelled as the rule's. The fix in PR #23/#24 is forward-only and trusts a stored rule_would_say verbatim, so this entry now survives every further --set. It self-heals only on a full re-triage of hyperspace.

Repair is one command -- ./tools/triage.sh hyperspace -- but it rewrites the whole ledger, so it wants its own PR where the diff can be read rather than being folded into an unrelated run.

Worth a sweep at the same time: any rule_would_say whose rule id cannot produce its verdict is the same fingerprint, and this may not be the only one.
acceptance_criteria: hyperspace's ledger regenerated; no entry in any ledger pairs a rule id with a verdict that rule cannot return

title: set_verdict attributes rule_would_say to a stale rule id
description:
Two low-severity attribution bugs in the rule_would_say recovery landed in a0e1074 (PR #24). Neither affects a verdict; both misname which rule produced one.

1. The fallback rule_id = entry['rule'] assumes entry['rule'] names the rule behind the entry's current verdict, but build_entries (triage_classify.py:409) deliberately preserves the *earlier* rule id for human entries and discards the fresh identifier. So: rule says A via a:pure, human overrides to B, the code changes so the rule now says B via b:nondeterministic, a full run sees agreement and drops rule_would_say while leaving rule: a:pure. A later --set C writes rule_would_say {B, a:pure} -- claiming the pure-function rule returned B, which it cannot do. The same stale id also skews the by_rule grouping in report().

2. The pop branch discards prior['rule'] without writing it back to entry['rule'], leaving the entry attributed to whatever id it happened to carry. Setting entry['rule'] = rule_id in that branch closes it.

Found by the second review pass on PR #24, after the merge.
acceptance_criteria: rule_would_say never names a rule id that cannot produce the verdict beside it; the pop branch restores entry['rule'] to the rule's own id

title: counts covers a different population in --set than in a full triage run
description:
The full run writes 'entries + stale' to the ledger but computes counts over 'entries' alone, so a function that no longer exists is stored but not counted. set_verdict() now recomputes counts (ss-xk6) over data['entries'], which is the stored list -- stale included.

The two therefore disagree whenever a ledger carries stale entries, and the counts block would flip between --set and a full run.

No ledger has stale entries today -- helios, hyperspace and hills all have counts summing exactly to their entry count -- so this is latent, not live. Deciding it needs an answer to what counts is for: the bucket split of work that exists (exclude stale) or a summary of the file (include them). Pick one and make both paths do it; a marker on carried-forward entries is the enabling change.
acceptance_criteria: both write paths compute counts over the same population, with the choice stated in the code
close_reason:
Fixed in review on PR #22 rather than deferred. The reviewer reproduced it against the real helios ledger -- appending one stale entry and running --set moved counts from 124 to 125 with no entry changing bucket, and the next full run silently reverts it. That is the same drift ss-xk6 fixed, one level up, and 'no ledger has stale entries today' was the wrong reason to defer when the tool keeps them indefinitely by design.

Resolution: the full run now marks carried-forward entries stale=True, and set_verdict summarises only the live ones. Both paths count the same population -- the work that exists -- by construction. Verified: with a stale entry present, --set holds counts at 124/23/67.

title: triage --set clobbers rule_would_say on a second override
description:
set_verdict() writes entry['rule_would_say'] = {previous verdict, previous rule} unconditionally. On the first human override that is correct -- the previous verdict is the rule's. On a second --set against the same entry it records the *human's* earlier verdict and calls it what the rule would say, which is false.

The field exists so a reader can see where the rules and a human disagree. Once it has been overwritten it no longer answers that.

Fix: only set it when entry.get('set_by') != 'human'. A full triage run already gets this right -- it regenerates rule_would_say from the fresh rule output at classify time.

Not hit by the ss-aio verdicts: all 38 entries were rule-set A before being set to B, so their rule_would_say is accurate.
acceptance_criteria: a second --set against an already-human entry leaves rule_would_say naming the rule's verdict
close_reason: Fixed across PR #23 (846a19d, the guard) and PR #24 (a0e1074, recovering the rule's verdict from the invariant when rule_would_say is absent). Seven cases verified through the real set_verdict; the set fails 4/7 against the pre-fix function and 2/7 against the first patch.

title: Guard misreads compound commands that switch branch then commit
description: guard-default-branch.py evaluates each git invocation against the branch at parse time, so 'git switch -c docs/x && git commit ...' is refused: the switch has not run yet so the commit still looks like a commit on main. Fails safe, and the workaround is splitting the commands, but it costs a retry every time. From L3-F6.

title: Measure the verifier's catch rate with planted bad tests
description: The verifier's effectiveness is assumed, not measured. Model diversity is now structural (verifier runs opus, authors run sonnet) which addresses correlated error, but nothing establishes that it actually catches tautological assertions, values copied from a run, or over-wide tolerances. A planted-bad-test fixture would turn the assumption into a number. This is P8 applied to the verifier. From L1-F2.

title: Deny write-shaped Bash for coverage-runner and verifier
description: P3 says nothing grades its own work, but both agents hold Bash and sed -i / echo > / git commit are all Bash. The restraint is instructed, with an after-the-fact tampering check (orchestrator compares HEAD and tree state across dispatch). A PreToolUse hook denying write-shaped Bash patterns for those two agent types would make it structural. Until then the doctrine must state the weaker truth, which it now does. From L1-F1.

title: triage_classify cannot see API coupling reached through a constructor
description:
The classifier reads each function's own source text to decide its verdict. That misses coupling a function inherits from an object it constructs.

Concrete case, found the expensive way in ss-aio: every impCubeVolume method is classified A, testable as-is, because none of them names a GL call. But impCubeVolume's constructor allocates an impSurface, whose constructor calls glGenBuffers, so none of them can run in a test binary at all. Roughly 300 regions were classified as available work that is not available.

A false A is the cheap direction to be wrong -- it wastes an attempt rather than deleting work from the queue the way a false C does -- but it is not free, and here it steered the phase-1 roadmap for a while.

Not obviously worth fixing in the rules. The skill already says they are deliberately regex rather than a parser, precise on linkage and API calls and weak on anything structural, and following construction chains is firmly on the parser side of that line. The cheaper answer may be to note the limit in the triage skill's 'What it cannot see' section, which already lists uninstantiated templates and #ifdef arms, and let human verdicts handle the cases.

Both copies now carry a human B verdict on makeSurface with rule_would_say preserved, so the disagreement is visible in the ledger diff.
design: Judgment call on scope. Detecting 'this function constructs a type whose constructor is api-coupled' needs the call graph, which is a different tool than the one that exists. Writing the limit down may be the whole fix.
close_reason: Documented in .claude/skills/triage/SKILL.md's 'What it cannot see' section rather than fixed in the rules, which was the outcome the issue's design note anticipated. Following construction chains needs the call graph, and the skill is explicit that these rules are deliberately regex rather than a parser. The section now carries the impCubeVolume case as the worked example and states the habit that actually prevents a recurrence: when a bucket-A entry is a member function, check what its constructor reaches, and the cheapest check is a test that only constructs the object.

title: rsQuat::slerp reads its own output in the antipodal branch
design:
Found while reading slerp to write ss-or3's tests. The covered branches -- the general acos path and the near-parallel shortcut -- are tested in helios PR #4 and hyperspace PR #3; this is the third branch, left alone.

Present in both helios and hyperspace: rsQuat.cpp differs between them only in include style.
acceptance_criteria: The antipodal branch produces a result that depends only on its inputs, and a test pins whatever that result is defined to be.
notes:
REALIGNED 2026-08-21 to the two-phase project shape. Belongs to the port rather than to phase 1.

Different from ss-4z1 and ss-wrt in one way that matters: this one is deliberately NOT pinned by a test. The antipodal branch's output depends on the destination quaternion's prior contents, so any assertion would encode one caller's leftovers rather than behaviour. There is no safety net here, which makes it the one of the three where the port has to be careful rather than merely deliberate.

Fixing it needs a decision about what the antipodal case should return, and the test comes with the fix.

title: rgb2hsl computes hue and saturation from raw channels, leaving rr/gg/bb dead
description:
rgb2hsl normalises the three channels into locals rr, gg and bb, divides them by luminosity, then desaturates them -- and never reads them again. Hue and saturation are computed from the raw r, g and b inputs instead. rr/gg/bb are dead stores.

Two visible consequences:

The rgb2hsl -> hsl2rgb round trip closes only where raw and normalised values coincide, which is fully saturated colours at full luminosity. rgb2hsl(0.5, 1.0, 0.2) round trips back to r = 0.6 rather than 0.5; luminosity and saturation are both correct in that case, so it is purely the hue that is wrong.

Mid grey reports saturation 0.5 rather than 0, because the saturation step computes s = 1.0f - b from the raw channel where 1.0f - bb was meant. The same substitution appears in all three huezone branches.

Present identically in helios and hyperspace.

## Steps to Reproduce

rgb2hsl(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, h, s, l) gives s = 0.5; an achromatic colour has no saturation.
rgb2hsl(0.5, 1.0, 0.2, ...) followed by hsl2rgb(h, s, l, ...) gives r = 0.6 for an input of 0.5.

Both pinned as CHARACTERIZATION cases in helios/tests/test_rgbhsl.cpp.
design: Same root cause for both symptoms, so one fix. Found while writing the first Rgbhsl coverage tests, helios PR #1.
acceptance_criteria: Hue and saturation derive from the normalised values; mid grey reports s = 0; the round trip closes for partially saturated colours; both characterization cases are replaced.
notes:
REALIGNED 2026-08-21 to the two-phase project shape. Same reasoning as ss-4z1: a behaviour decision belonging to the port, not standalone maintenance.

Pinned by two characterization cases, rgb2hsl_does_not_round_trip_partially_saturated_colours and rgb2hsl_saturation_uses_the_raw_channel_not_the_normalised_one, in both helios and hyperspace. Those are the safety net for the port, and the reason this can safely wait.

title: rgb2hsl reads luminosity from the wrong channel in huezones 2 and 3
description:
rgb2hsl sorts its input into one of six huezones, then a switch reads luminosity off the channel that zone says is largest. The grouping is {0,5}->r, {1,2}->g, {3,4}->b, and two of those are wrong.

Zone 2 is r<g with b>g, where blue is the largest channel, but it is grouped with 1 and gets l=g. Zone 3 is r<g with r<b<=g, where green is largest, but it is grouped with 4 and gets l=b. The correct grouping is {1,3}->g and {2,4}->b.

For any colour landing in those zones, l comes back as neither the largest channel nor anything else meaningful, and the rgb2hsl -> hsl2rgb round trip cannot close.

Present identically in helios and hyperspace (shared_copy: identical on the Rgbhsl entries).

## Steps to Reproduce

rgb2hsl(0.25, 0.5, 0.8, h, s, l) gives l = 0.5; the largest channel is 0.8.
rgb2hsl(0.25, 0.9, 0.5, h, s, l) gives l = 0.5; the largest channel is 0.9.

Both are pinned by rgb2hsl_luminosity_is_wrong_in_huezones_two_and_three in helios/tests/test_rgbhsl.cpp, which is a CHARACTERIZATION case and will fail when this is fixed. Replace it with the largest-channel expectation rather than retuning it.
design: Found while writing the first coverage tests for Rgbhsl, helios PR #1. Left unfixed there deliberately so the tests land first and the fix has something to move against.
acceptance_criteria: l equals max(r,g,b) for every input; the round trip closes for colours in zones 2 and 3; the characterization case is replaced.
notes:
REALIGNED 2026-08-21 to the two-phase project shape.

This is not phase 1 work and should not be fixed as standalone maintenance. It is a behaviour decision that belongs to the port of the submodule that contains it (ss-z2c for helios, ss-a4a for hyperspace).

The reasoning: the decision already taken was to leave it characterized rather than fix it, because fixing it changes what the savers render and the current output is arguably the spec for 20-year-old vendored code. Under phase 2 that decision gets made anyway -- the port touches this code, and at that point you either preserve the behaviour deliberately or change it deliberately. Doing it now would be a rendering change with no port to justify it; doing it never would leave an undocumented trap.

What phase 1 already contributed here is the thing that matters: rgb2hsl_luminosity_is_wrong_in_huezones_two_and_three pins the current behaviour in both submodules and says what correct would be. That test is the safety net. If the port changes this by accident, the test fails; if it changes it on purpose, the test gets replaced.

title: Narrow the gh pr permission so merging is a deliberate act
description:
.claude/settings.local.json pre-approves Bash(gh pr *), which includes gh pr merge. Meanwhile no repo in the project has any server-side review gate today -- verified in both audits: no .github/workflows anywhere, no branch protection, and the already-merged screen-savers PR #3 shows empty statusCheckRollup, reviewDecision and latestReviews. So the freehand merge path is wide open in a design that treats independent review as load-bearing.

Narrow the allow entry to the read and create verbs, or add Bash(gh pr merge:*) to permissions.deny in settings.json, which takes precedence.

State the limit honestly when doing it: this constrains only the hand-typed path. A merge performed inside a script is invisible to the permission layer, the same blindness that makes the proposed gh pr merge hook clause unable to fire. This is honest friction, not a gate.
design: Low priority precisely because of that limit -- it is worth doing, but it should not be mistaken for the review gate the superproject still lacks.
acceptance_criteria: gh pr merge prompts for approval rather than running pre-approved.
close_reason: Closed

title: Record the decision not to add a gh pr merge clause to guard-default-branch.py
description:
The harness build instructions propose adding a clause to guard-default-branch.py that blocks gh pr merge when the tree is dirty or the head branch has unpushed commits. Two independent audits reached the same conclusion: it cannot fire, and the effort belongs elsewhere.

Why it cannot fire. The PreToolUse hook matches Bash and reads tool_input.command. Any gh pr merge run by a ship script executes inside that script, so the hook sees ./tools/ship.sh helios and nothing more. It would only ever catch a hand-typed gh pr merge -- the exact thing the harness design says the orchestrator has stopped doing. It is also not a clause: parse() yields only invocations whose argv[0] basename is git, so this would be a structural rewrite of the hook. And the dirty-tree and unpushed-commit checks would inspect the wrong repository, since the hook resolves cwd from the payload while a ship script cds into the submodule internally.

Why it is unnecessary anyway. The case it targets -- merging a PR that does not contain what is on disk -- cannot arise in a script that pushes before it polls. The genuinely new risk a ship harness introduces is merging before review, and a PreToolUse hook cannot see that either.

Write the decision down where the hook lives so it is not re-proposed.
design: Sources: ship-harness-audit.md section 7 and harness-build-instructions-review.md section 6, reached independently. The recommended alternative -- asserting branch protection at preflight -- is tracked separately as the superproject review-gate decision.
acceptance_criteria: A comment or note in the hook or its docs states the clause was evaluated and rejected, with the reason.
close_reason: Closed

title: Give the closed C-set an amendment process
description:
The triage skill closes the C reason set -- c:compiler-generated, c:trivial-accessor, c:generated-table, c:vendored-unmodified -- which is right, since an open-ended not worth it becomes a place to put anything inconvenient. But lines 58-60 say a new reason is discussed, not a one-off without naming a venue. A constitution with no amendment clause fails a particular way: legitimate new categories accumulate in the ? bucket, resolved one verdict at a time, and the pressure to misfile into an existing C grows.

The evidence an amendment needs is already being collected -- human --set verdicts keep rule_would_say when they disagree with the rules. Write the clause into the skill: when three or more human verdicts share a rationale no existing rule captures, that is a proposal for a new closed-set member, filed as a pull request against the rule table in tools/triage_classify.py citing those ledger entries as evidence.

The same paragraph should name where the doctrine itself gets amended. It is currently stated across five files with no designated seat, so a principle that loses an argument with reality has nowhere to be revised.
design: Source: refinements/doctrine-errors.md point 6.
acceptance_criteria: The triage skill names a threshold, a venue and an evidence source for adding a C reason.
close_reason: Closed

title: Derive the loop's stop decision from loop-log rather than a fixed cap
description:
Two related gaps in Stage 5's decision table.

The hard cap of 3 iterations is fixed by impression, in prose, forever -- in a design whose stated reason for keeping loop-log is that is this working gets answered with data rather than impression. A loop still improving at iteration 3 stops; one that plateaued at 2 already wasted an iteration. Replace the addressable did not improve row with a marginal-gain floor read from loop-log -- stop when the iteration's addressable gain falls below a floor -- and keep 3 as the outer bound rather than the rule. The log already records addressable per iteration; the data is there and simply unused.

Escalation is only a success if escalations get consumed. The loop files a bd issue per blocked entry but models no human capacity, so it has no answer to a backlog of successful escalations nobody reads. Add to Stage 0: if open escalation issues from prior runs exceed a threshold, stop and report -- another run would add to a pile rather than to coverage.
design: Source: refinements/doctrine-errors.md point 5. The point is self-application: a system built on answer with data has not turned that principle on its own stop rule.
acceptance_criteria: The stop decision reads a number out of loop-log. Stage 0 refuses to start on an unconsumed escalation backlog.
close_reason: Closed

title: Unblock parallel test-writers within a single submodule
description: /coverage-loop serializes test-writer dispatch within one submodule because the agents share one working tree and one git index, and because tools/coverage.sh hardcodes BUILD_ROOT=.coverage-build and does 'rm -rf' on it at the start of every build. Two concurrent gate runs against the same submodule destroy each other. Unblocking it needs two changes: a COVERAGE_BUILD_ROOT (or --build-dir) override in coverage.sh, and a per-writer git worktree of the submodule so drafts do not collide. Only worth doing if wall-clock in the loop turns out to matter.
design: Cross-submodule parallelism already works and is what the loop uses today; this is about the within-submodule case.

title: Decide hyperspace impCubeVolume::polygonize triage verdict
description: The classifier cannot isolate polygonize's body because #if USE_TRIANGLE_STRIPS splits the loop across preprocessor arms, so it sits in the ? bucket awaiting a human call. The identical function in helios was judged A. Record with: tools/triage.sh hyperspace --set 'impCubeVolume::polygonize(unsigned int)' --verdict A --reason '...'
close_reason: Merged as fiazsami/screen-savers PR #9. Recorded verdict A with rule_would_say preserved. The call was the helios twin's existing human verdict applied to a byte-identical body (same md5 over the function), not a fresh judgment.
